In brief

After the testosterone poisoning of Cyclops, the first few paragraphs of Nausicaa are nauseatingly feminine. Relentlessly upbeat, romantic, cutesy, and clichéd, they sound like an exceptionally bad sentimental novel—as far a leap as one could imagine from the idiomatic bite, misanthropic bile, drunken intensity, and acerbic laughter of the preceding chapter. But the two techniques have at least one thing in common: an insistence on falsifying experience. The Cyclops parodies exaggerate styles of speech and writing so greatly that their truth-claims seem risible. The first couple of pages of Nausicaa sound like a continuation of this parodic mode, and they too show themselves to be exercises in misrepresentation. For anyone who reads with even a smidgen of critical scrutiny, their phrases repeatedly fail to stand up to scrutiny. After about two pages the rose-colored prologue gives way to a more subdued prose style, but some of the air of falseness remains.

At more length

The first sentence cultivates an air of erotic romance: "The summer evening had begun to fold the world in its mysterious embrace." Outside of bodice-rippers, are embraces ever "mysterious"? And what human being has ever regarded a summer evening as a lover? The next sentence continues the implausible metaphor: "the last glow of all too fleeting day lingered lovingly on sea and strand." People may lovingly cherish the ends of beautiful evenings, but evenings do not reciprocate. And should long summer evenings really be called "fleeting"? The evening rays linger on sea, strand, Howth Head (why exactly is it "proud"? why is it "guarding" the bay"?), weedy rocks, and, "last but not least," the local church. Last but not least: is the church a beauty pageant contestant that the evening light sees as a potential winner? Is the light captivated by the praises of Mary going on inside because she too is a kind of light ("a beacon ever to the stormtossed heart of man")? What kind of a love story is this, anyhow?

Nature is not just romantically anthropomorphized but also prettified. The narrative reports that three girls often come to their "favourite nook to have a cosy chat beside the sparkling waves and discuss matters feminine." The "weedgrown rocks" on which they are sitting don't much resemble a domestic "nook," and though some days may boast sparkling waves beside the rocks, 16 June 1904 could not. On that day low tide came at 6:29 PM and high tide did not arrive until after midnight, so what the women are actually looking at is a vast stretch of mud flats. Nothing they do there could be described as "a cosy chat."

A reader's sense that matters are being falsified continues as the narrative confides that the little boys are "very noisy and spoiled twins sometimes," but then maintains, in the same sentence, that they are also "darling little fellows with bright merry faces and endearing ways about them." One suspects that whoever is telling this tale cannot long maintain the thought that children are anything other than innocent angels—much like the editors who changed Emily Dickinson's "Children Strove At Recess—in the Ring" to "played at recess." The boys play with sand castles and a beach ball "happy as the day was long." But hasn't the day just been called all too fleeting? And the "slight altercation between Master Tommy and Master Jacky" that happens shortly later—actually a bitter fight—suggests that their happiness does not last long either.

The narrator reaches first for a cliché to excuse the boys' squabble and then for grand analogues to ennoble it: "Boys will be boys and our two twins were no exception to this golden rule. The apple of discord was a certain castle of sand." The golden rule of Matthew 7:12, Do unto others as you would have them do unto you, has no application whatsoever to the banal saying that boys will be boys, while the apple of discord, a story from Greek mythology, inflates their disagreement into a struggle comparable to the Trojan war. Eris, the goddess of strife and discord, threw down an apple that she said was meant for the most beautiful goddess. The resulting contest between Aphrodite, Hera, and Athena ended with Paris awarding the apple to Aphrodite. She rewarded him in turn with Menelaus's wife Helen. And the rest was boys being boys.

The people are painted in precious colors. When Edy Boardman rocks the baby in his pram, "that young gentleman fairly chuckled with delight." Characterizing a baby as a grown man is merely revolting. Making him "chuckle" borders on disturbing. Cissy Caffrey seems like an agreeable and entertaining young woman, but those qualities are hard to discern through the thick impasto of clichés applied to her: "A truerhearted lass never drew the breath of life, always with a laugh in her gipsylike eyes and a frolicsome word on her cherryripe red lips, a girl lovable in the extreme." Ripe-cherry lips must have felt distressingly unrealistic to some listeners even when Thomas Campion, William Shakespeare, and Robert Herrick put them in their verses. Deployed three hundred years later, they are a mockery. Nor does painting Cissy as a seductive Carmen make her spring to life on the page. Is love "in the extreme" a good thing?

When Gerty MacDowell enters the narrative its style changes markedly, swinging into her orbit by the principle of free indirect discourse. From this point on the prose is much less over-the-top. To be sure, plenty of clichés remain. Gerty thinks that married love "would be like heaven" and calls up familiar airy sayings about it: "Love laughs at locksmiths. She would make the great sacrifice." She thinks of her father in "the clutches of the demon drink," and abominates "that vile decoction which has ruined so many hearths and homes." And false notes continue to ring out: the ads for female beauty products that Gerty consumes religiously, and the childhood fairy tales on which she models her romantic hopes. But the writing is now focused on her thoughts and feelings, propelled by erotic reverie rather than pretty scene-painting. And now a more compelling source of romantic phrasings can be discerned: Joyce's earlier writing about his own erotic reveries.

It is hard to know exactly how to respond to the strongly feminized first half of Nausicaa. Certainly it invites some mockery, especially in response to those two saccharine opening pages. But any suspicion of misogynistic contempt on Joyce's part must be tempered by awareness of how much of himself he put into Gerty. The implied criticism of her callow idealism is significantly different, but not completely different, from the criticism of Stephen's callow idealism in A Portrait of the Artist and the early chapters of Ulysses.

John Hunt 2026
